title: reagent-migration: MIG-23 cold SSR boot omits mandatory adapter initialization
description:
## Scope

Correct the MIG-23 Reagent-to-Hicasso SSR migration guidance in skills/reagent-migration/references/catalog-judgment.md and its behavioural contract in skills/reagent-migration/evals/evals.json. Add focused cold-start evidence for the recipe. Keep the shipped Hicasso/SSR runtime APIs and adapter-selection policy unchanged.

## Correctness finding

MIG-23 calls the server half "one call" and shows server/render in a fresh app.server namespace with no rf/init!, then calls the client half exactly three ordered calls beginning with rf/make-frame, again with no rf/init!. Both paths construct a frame. re-frame2 has no default adapter registry: frame construction delegates to the installed adapter's make-state-container and raises :rf.error/no-adapter-installed in a never-initialized process.

This is especially easy to hit in the migration the rule recommends: the Node renderer is a separate process from the browser, so an adapter installed by client boot cannot satisfy server boot. Copying the skill's server recipe into the newly introduced Node service fails before React renders a document; copying the client recipe into a cold entry fails before state hydration. The same skill already states the invariant correctly for MIG-15 and eval 25, but MIG-23 and eval 23 omit it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start a fresh Node CLJS process with the MIG-23 server namespace and no prior rf/init!, using a minimal deterministic hiccup root and a valid non-empty payload policy.
2. Call the shown server/render expression.
3. Observe that server/render calls rf/make-frame, which throws :rf.error/no-adapter-installed at rf/make-state-container; no :document is returned.
4. In a separate fresh browser/DOM test process, run the shown client function with no prior rf/init!.
5. Observe that its first rf/make-frame throws the same error, so ssr/hydrate! and h/hydrate! never run.
6. Install ssr/adapter once in the server process and a supported React-shaped adapter once in the client process. The otherwise identical server and client frame entry points advance, isolating the missing boot precondition.

## Evidence

- skills/reagent-migration/references/catalog-judgment.md lines 352-361 says "The server half is one call" and shows server/render with no re-frame.core or adapter require and no rf/init!.
- The same file lines 370-378 says "The client half is THREE ordered calls" and begins with rf/make-frame; no adapter is installed before it.
- skills/reagent-migration/evals/evals.json lines 112-120 grades that exact MIG-23 pipeline. Expectation 116 requires the three ordered client calls, but no expectation preserves or installs an adapter in either process.
- implementation/hicasso/src/re_frame/hicasso/server.cljs lines 137-198 implements server/render and calls rf/make-frame for every request.
- implementation/core/src/re_frame/frame.cljc lines 2371-2383 constructs a frame through adapter/make-state-container. implementation/core/src/re_frame/substrate/adapter.cljc lines 327-351 makes the cold path a structured :rf.error/no-adapter-installed throw and explicitly says rf/init! must run first.
- implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/substrate.cljc documents (rf/init! ssr/adapter) as the server-side installation. implementation/hicasso/src/re_frame/hicasso/substrate.cljs lines 1-3 and 139-145 likewise says a Hicasso adapter is installed before the first frame.
- skills/reagent-migration/evals/evals.json line 138 and references/catalog-mechanical.md's MIG-15 already carry the correct rule: nothing installs an adapter automatically, and a migrating app keeps its existing Reagent adapter. MIG-23 is internally inconsistent with that known invariant.

## Failure scenario / invariant

A programmer accepts MIG-23's infrastructure decision and stands up the Node renderer it recommends. In the new process they paste the complete-looking server namespace and call server/render. The call reaches rf/make-frame, which reaches rf/make-state-container with no installed adapter and throws :rf.error/no-adapter-installed; no HTML, payload, or document is returned. On the browser side, the shown run function fails at its first rf/make-frame for the same reason if no earlier boot code happened to install an adapter.

Invariant: every process that constructs a frame must install exactly one appropriate adapter with rf/init! before its first frame. A migration recipe must preserve the existing Reagent adapter on the browser unless the programmer chooses otherwise, and must explicitly initialize the separate Node process (normally with the SSR adapter) before any server/render request.

## Recommended minimal fix

Keep the three hydration operations and their ordering, but state and show the adapter installation as the boot precondition immediately before them. On the client, retain the app's existing (rf/init! reagent-adapter/adapter) before rf/make-frame; do not silently switch a part-migrated app to another adapter. On the new Node service, require re-frame.core and re-frame.ssr and install ssr/adapter once at process startup before the first server/render call, not once per request. A Hicasso-only application may deliberately choose re-frame.hicasso.substrate/adapter on the client, but adapter selection is not part of this migration.

Update eval 23 so an answer that emits the current cold recipes without both process boot preconditions fails grading. Preserve the server/render -> ssr/hydrate! -> h/hydrate! pipeline and all existing frame-id, payload-policy, and identifier-prefix guidance.

## Acceptance Criteria

- MIG-23's server example is executable from a never-initialized Node process: it installs an appropriate server adapter once before the first server/render, then the existing render call returns a document and hydration payload.
- MIG-23's client example explicitly keeps/installs the migrating app's existing Reagent adapter before rf/make-frame, followed by the existing ordered state-hydrate and DOM-adopt calls. The prose distinguishes adapter initialization from the three hydration operations rather than deleting or reordering those operations.
- Eval 23 gains an explicit cold two-process condition and grades both requirements: server adapter initialization before server/render and client adapter initialization before rf/make-frame. It must continue to reject claims that the shipped render/hydrate doors are absent.
- Focused executable cold-start coverage resets adapter lifecycle to the never-installed state and proves the current recipe is non-vacuously red: server/render and client rf/make-frame each raise :rf.error/no-adapter-installed before any render/hydration work. Positive controls install ssr/adapter for the server and a supported React-shaped adapter for the client, then prove the same frame/render entry points advance successfully.
- A control proves initialization is process boot, not request/reload work: two server/render requests after one server rf/init! do not attempt a second adapter install, and the client hydration/HMR path does not re-run rf/init!.
- The MIG-15 mount guidance and eval 25 continue to keep the existing Reagent adapter; no answer is graded toward an unsolicited adapter switch.
- Run the reagent-migration eval/package checks and the focused Hicasso server/frame cold-start tests successfully.

## Non-goals

- No default adapter, implicit installation, server/render auto-installation, or change to rf/make-frame.
- No mandatory switch from the existing Reagent adapter to Hicasso's adapter during a partial migration.
- No SSR pipeline, payload-policy, frame-id, identifier-prefix, or hydration-order redesign.
- No broad rewrite of Hicasso installation documentation or unrelated migration rules.
- No compatibility layer for code that already bootstraps an adapter elsewhere.

## Related / duplicate search

Searched all-status bead titles and descriptions for reagent migration, MIG-23, SSR hydration, server/render, adapter init, rf/init!, no-adapter-installed, cold boot, Node renderer, and Hicasso SSR. No issue owns this skill recipe failure. Closed rf2-v4yfr introduced the now-shipped MIG-23 pipeline and deliberately established its three hydration calls, but did not cover adapter initialization. Closed rf2-ttmi9 established the general Hicasso boot invariant in installation/cookbook docs, not this skill or its two-process SSR eval. Closed rf2-4zkbd corrected the obsolete claim that Hicasso has no adapter and retained rf/init! for MIG-15/eval 25; it did not apply that requirement to MIG-23. These are provenance and positive controls, not duplicates.
acceptance_criteria: MIG-23 and eval 23 show/grade one adapter initialization per cold runtime before frame construction: ssr/adapter before the Node service's first server/render and the existing Reagent adapter before the browser's rf/make-frame, followed by the unchanged state-hydrate then DOM-adopt order. A focused cold-start control proves both current omissions raise :rf.error/no-adapter-installed, positive controls advance after installation, repeated requests/reload do not reinstall, and the reagent-migration plus focused Hicasso server/frame tests pass.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #8838 (worker/mig23-ssr-init-vpdrf, head 8bbd8110b3, ready for review): MIG-23 in skills/reagent-migration/references/catalog-judgment.md now states the cold two-process boot invariant — the server half installs (rf/init! ssr/adapter) once at process startup before the first server/render, the client half keeps the migrating app's existing Reagent adapter (MIG-15's line) as boot precondition step 0 ahead of the unchanged three ordered hydration calls, install is per process not per load, adapter selection stays out of scope. evals.json eval 23 gains two expectations grading the cold two-process condition and the no-silent-adapter-switch precondition; door-exists rejections unchanged. Executable cold-start evidence at skills/reagent-migration/tests/fixture/ (shadow-cljs :node-test over the in-repo implementation via :local/root): never-initialized negatives at server/render and rf/make-frame both raise :rf.error/no-adapter-installed, positive server control (one init!, two renders, adapter-spec identity unchanged), client-shaped positive (Reagent adapter advances make-frame; reload init! re-run is a no-op) — 1 test, 12 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors. Gates on the final rebased base, captured exits: fixture compile 0, fixture run 0, check_skill_eval_docs 0, check_skill_eval_packaging (self-test 0, ci 0), check_skill_package_refs (self-test 0, ci 0), check_doc_slugs 0, check_readme_links --ci 0; planted-fault proofs went red naming the planted line (doc_slugs exit 1 on a broken link in the edited paragraph; eval_docs exit 1 on a duplicated eval id), restores blob-hash-verified. Follow-ups filed: rf2-bbe91 (wire fixture into skills-structural CI), rf2-byig6 (docs ch18 same cold-boot gap). Implementation/runtime APIs untouched.

title: surface-review(implementation-build): let Node discover the script test suite
description:
## Scope

Replace the hand-maintained file rosters behind `implementation/package.json`'s `test:script-policy` and `test:script-helpers` with one canonical implementation-level JavaScript harness command. Cover the 42 conventionally named `implementation/scripts/*.test.cjs` files, the two intended out-of-tree `.test.cjs` support tests currently in the helpers chain, and the native-IME verdict self-test. Update the fast-PR, CI, documentation, and policy consumers that currently know the two-command spelling. Preserve each test file's behaviour, process isolation, and failure signal.

## Findings

The suite already has a complete naming convention but does not use it. `implementation/scripts/` contains 42 `*.test.cjs` files. `test:script-policy` names 34 of them one by one; `test:script-helpers` names the other 8, plus two out-of-tree `.test.cjs` files and one CLI `--self-test`. That is 45 literal `node` invocations across two 2,218-character package-script values. Every new conventional test needs a second registration edit to one contested JSON line.

The split has user-visible cost without an execution boundary. The fast spine and CI always chain both commands. `TESTING.md` records that running only the second half has already let a red through. `scripts/check_fast_pr_gap.py` therefore pins the exact two-command string, and `implementation/scripts/_reagent-slim-smoke-policy.test.cjs` parses `package.json` to assert that its own filename appears in the roster. These are guards around manual registration rather than product or test semantics.

History shows the mechanism repeatedly failing in the dark direction. Closed beads `rf2-z2xir`, `rf2-45ti9`, `rf2-9ayub`, `rf2-lr4id`, and `rf2-zu82n` each existed to append tests or self-tests that had landed but ran in no spine; their notes also record guaranteed conflicts because each insertion rewrote the same long `package.json` line. The recent bench retirement removed most exceptional flag-driven readers, leaving only one such CLI self-test in the current helpers command, so this is now a small simplification rather than a framework project.

CI pins Node 24. Node 24's built-in test runner discovers quoted `*.test.cjs` glob patterns, runs each matching file in an isolated child process, and treats the child's exit code as the file verdict; files are explicitly not required to use `node:test` internally. The existing standalone harness files can therefore retain their current code and output. `--test-concurrency=1` can preserve today's serial host-load posture.

## Recommended Action

Create one obvious command, `npm run test:scripts`, that uses the Node 24 test runner with quoted, repository-scoped glob patterns for the conventional `.test.cjs` populations and `--test-concurrency=1`. Keep `scripts/run-hicasso-native-ime-witness.cjs --self-test` as the one explicit prelude, or expose that verdict control through a tiny conventional `.test.cjs` wrapper; do not build a custom discovery runner.

Delete `test:script-policy` and `test:script-helpers` rather than retain forwarding aliases. Point the fast spine, the `js-harness-self-tests` CI job, `TESTING.md`, and `scripts/check_fast_pr_gap.py` at the single command. Remove self-enrolment assertions and comments that tell authors to edit `package.json`; adding a correctly named test file should be the registration act.

## Evidence

- `implementation/package.json:60-61` contains the two literal rosters: 34 policy files and 11 helper invocations.
- `rg --files implementation/scripts -g '*.test.cjs'` returns 42 files; all 42 occur exactly once across those two package scripts. The helper command separately names `core/test/re_frame/bench/lane_cache_wiring.test.cjs`, `hicasso/scripts/check_modules_compile.test.cjs`, and the native-IME `--self-test`.
- `TESTING.md:20` presents both names as one JS-harness tier; `TESTING.md:181-183` says they must be chained and records that running only the second let a red through.
- `scripts/test-fast-pr.sh:1489-1490` and `.github/workflows/test.yml:3131` duplicate the chained spelling; `scripts/check_fast_pr_gap.py:297` pins it as an exact regular expression.
- `implementation/scripts/_reagent-slim-smoke-policy.test.cjs:203-208` checks its own textual enrolment in `test:script-policy`.
- Closed registration beads `rf2-z2xir`, `rf2-45ti9`, `rf2-9ayub`, `rf2-lr4id`, and `rf2-zu82n` document tests that existed but were not executed, plus contention on the one-line roster.
- Node 24 documentation lists `**/*.test.cjs` as a default discovery shape, recommends quoted globs for portability, and states that isolated test files are judged by process exit code without needing to use `node:test`: https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v24.x/api/test.html#running-tests-from-the-command-line
- Exact tracker searches for `node --test`, `auto-discover`, `test:script-policy`, `test:script-helpers`, `hand-register`, and `surface-review(implementation-build)` found no open, in-progress, or deferred bead owning this outcome.

## Acceptance Criteria

- From `implementation/`, one documented `npm run test:scripts` command runs the same 44 `.test.cjs` files and the same native-IME verdict self-test that the two old commands run today, each exactly once.
- The command uses Node's built-in discovery over explicit repository-scoped globs, with process isolation and concurrency 1; it adds no dependency and no custom file-inventory runner.
- A temporary failing `implementation/scripts/*-negative-control.test.cjs` is discovered without editing `package.json`, makes the command exit non-zero, and is named in the failure output; removing it restores green. Record the red/green control in the PR.
- Baseline and replacement runs agree on the executed file population and preserve actionable stdout/stderr from a deliberately failing existing fixture or equivalent scoped mutation.
- `test:script-policy` and `test:script-helpers` are removed, not retained as aliases. The fast spine, `js-harness-self-tests` CI job, `TESTING.md`, and fast-PR gap check all use the one canonical command.
- The self-enrolment assertion in `_reagent-slim-smoke-policy.test.cjs` and stale comments telling authors to wire individual `.test.cjs` files into `package.json` are deleted or rewritten to describe convention-based discovery.
- The focused command passes on Windows and in the Node 24 Linux CI job without increasing test-file concurrency or introducing shared-fixture collisions.

## Non-goals

- Rewriting the 44 standalone test files to the `node:test` API or changing their assertion harnesses.
- Parallelising test files, changing their internal order, suppressing their diagnostics, or weakening exit-code handling.
- Auto-running every arbitrary `--self-test` mode in the repository; only conventional `.test.cjs` files are discovered, with the one current exceptional CLI control handled explicitly or wrapped conventionally.
- Folding CLJS, browser, JVM, API-manifest, bundle, benchmark, or rigorous-local suites into this command.
- Adding a watcher, third-party test framework, generated manifest, or new inventory/policy checker.

## Related beads

- `rf2-z2xir`, `rf2-45ti9`, `rf2-9ayub`, `rf2-lr4id`, and `rf2-zu82n` are closed instances of the manual-registration failure this task removes; none replaces this outcome.
- `rf2-fal5` is closed Windows host-load work inside `test:script-policy`; preserving serial process isolation respects that evidence but does not reopen or redesign the classifier suite.
- `rf2-6c12m.1` is the closed bench re-home/retirement that removed most exceptional helper registrations and made convention-based discovery a bounded change.
- No open, in-progress, deferred, or closed bead found in the tracker proposes replacing the two rosters with native Node discovery.

description:

The real error was narrower: the measurements excluded .beads and the control did not, so the two searched different corpora. Match the exclusion set on both sides.

THE PROTOCOL FAILURE THIS FIXES, measured the same day. Worker A announced RELEASING and promised to announce before re-taking; the mayor told worker B the lane was free; B announced TAKING; A then announced RE-TAKING exactly as promised. Nobody broke the rule and the lane was doubly held. ANNOUNCE-AND-TAKE IS NOT A LOCK: an announcement NOTIFIES and does not ASK, so two correct announcements compose into a collision.

WHAT LANDED IN CLAUDE.md: the fact, the measurement, and the arbitration rules -- first acquirer holds; never grant on a release message alone; grant explicitly to one worker and keep a queue; a yielding worker kills its run and verifies by effect; tell the yielding worker whose fault it was; a worker that overlapped says so, and the holder re-runs rather than debugging. Plus the generalising sentence: a rule phrased as "announce X" tells you what to SAY and not what to CHECK, and where two holders means silent destruction the protocol needs a step that can REFUSE.

After the merge the mayor ran the three-number line-ending check against `git show origin/main:CLAUDE.md` -- the BLOB -- and read cr=0 crlf=0 bare_lf=157, which the check duly reported as PROBLEM. ## The problem, carefully

**The promise.** `spec/Conventions.md:1054`, in `### Routes are prisms (deferred to Spec 012)`:

> Registered route patterns define a lawful partial round trip (a *prism*) between URLs and route data — `match-url(route-url(...))` returns canonical route data, **query keys are emitted in deterministic canonical order**, `nil` query values are elided, and out-of-domain params fail closed.

That is the ONLY normative home. `spec/012-Routing.md` §Bidirectional URL ↔ params (:750-768) does not carry it — the one "order" in that range (:759) is about bad address keys being *reported* in canonical order, against a control of 42 "order" hits in the file. The original review (rf2-pk4i6.7 finding 4) and the rf2-17bbi bullet both located it in 012; the sweep worker measured that it is not there, which is why the item stopped and became this bead.

**The code.** Three sites in `implementation/routing/src/re_frame/routing/registry.cljc` seed a sorted sequence into `(array-map)`:

- `canonical-query-order` :1032-1033 — the INBOUND leg: reorders `match-url`'s `:query` after parse (called at :1355).
- `query-without-defaults` :1113-1115 — drops keys at their declared default on the OUTBOUND leg (called at :2198).
- `emitted-query` inside `route-url` :1849-1852 — the OUTBOUND sort (`sort-by (comp rf.identity/canonical-bytes key)`).

The URL string is then `map`/`join` over `url-query` (:2218-2230), so the order of `?k=v` pairs is whatever that map iterates. Two further `(array-map)` reduce seeds (:1003 `coerce-query`, :1288 the raw parse) promote the same way but sit UPSTREAM of the inbound sort, so they are irrelevant to the promise. `canonical-bytes` tags the key kind: `:page` sorts as `"k::page"`, `"page"` as `"s:\"page\""` (probe 2), so keyword keys sort before string keys and alphabetically within a kind.

**The mechanism, measured by me on this tree** (`clojure -M <probe>` from `implementation/routing`, reproducing the bead's figures exactly):

```
 8 keys  (into (array-map) pairs) -> clojure.lang.PersistentArrayMap  order-preserved? true
 9 keys  (into (array-map) pairs) -> clojure.lang.PersistentHashMap   order-preserved? false  [:k02 :k06 :k07 :k03 :k05 :k09 :k01 :k04 :k08]
12 keys  (into (array-map) pairs) -> clojure.lang.PersistentHashMap   order-preserved? false  [:k11 :k12 :k02 :k06 :k07 :k03 :k05 :k09 :k10 :k01 :k04 :k08]
 9/12    (apply array-map (mapcat identity pairs)) -> PersistentArrayMap, order-preserved? true
```

**Who repeats the promise (everything that must move together under (A)).** `deterministic canonical order` reads 14 lines in 9 tracked files (ripgrep; `.beads/issues.jsonl` excluded), two of which the bead does not list:

| `registry.cljc:1007-1009` | `canonical-query-order` docstring: "deterministic CEDN-1 canonical KEY order … return an array-map so the order is stable downstream" |
| `registry.cljc:1021` and `:1826-1839` | comments quoting the Conventions sentence verbatim |
| `spec/conformance/fixtures/routing-match-url.edn:66-70`, `:97-103`; `routing-query-string-coercion.edn:112-116` | fixture comments quoting it; the fixtures themselves pin TWO-key URLs (`/search?page=2&q=clojure`) |
| `implementation/routing/test/re_frame/routing_registry_test.clj:672-677` | test comment; the deftest pins two- and three-key URLs |
| `routing_prism_property_cljs_test.cljc:22-26` | property-test header: "CANONICAL QUERY KEY ORDER — both prism legs share ONE canonical order" |

**Why no test caught it.** The both-hosts property test's `gen-query` draws 0..3 pairs (`(rnd state 4)`, :118-119), and no test or fixture anywhere carries a URL with 9+ query pairs: a census for 8+ `&` under `implementation/routing/test/**` and `spec/conformance/fixtures/**` reads 0, against a control of 26 hits for 2+ `&`. So (B) breaks no existing test, and (A) changes no test.

**Is anything actually broken today? No — and this is the practical stake.** Measured on a real registered route (probe 1 and 2, JVM):

- Route DATA is order-blind. `match-url(route-url(q12))` returns `:query` equal to the 12-key input (`=`), `:validation-failed? false`; `identical-route-target?` compares `:route-id`/`:params`/`:query`/`:fragment` with `=` (`plan.cljc:94-97`), so no-op detection is unaffected; `:query-defaults` still elide and fill back at 10 keys.
- Same map → same URL, still. The same 12 keys inserted in REVERSED order emit the byte-identical URL today (a hash map's iteration order depends on the key set, not insertion order). The property consumers actually rely on — stable href for caching/dedupe, spelling-independence — holds.
- The URL-string leg of the prism reproduces at 12 keys when the route DECLARES its `:query` keys (keyword keys both sides: `route-url(match-url(u)) = u`, probe 2). It does NOT reproduce for an UNDECLARED 12-key query, because `match-url` hands back string keys and strings hash to a different trie order than keywords (probe 1). But `routing-match-url.edn:97-103` already states the string leg holds "only when its keys are already in canonical order", so this is the existing modulo-permutation caveat, not a new law violation.
- Cross-host: the reviewer's and bead's claim that the same key set iterates identically on JVM and CLJS ("same hashes, same trie") is ASSERTED, not measured by anyone — no CLJS probe was permitted here. It matters only for an SSR-rendered `href` with 9+ query keys that the client re-renders; the SSR artefact itself never calls `route-url` (`ssr.cljc:402` is a comment), so this would be an app's own `[:a {:href (rf.routing/route-url …)}]` on both hosts. I could find no code in `routing/src` that compares two URL strings for equality (`\((not)?= …url…` reads only `history.cljc:220`, a strategy comparison, and `scroll.cljc:81`, a cache key rebuilt from the slice on one host; control: the property test's `(not= url url')` reads 1).

So the stakes are the STATED promise and its ergonomic value (a hand-readable, sorted query string), not behaviour.

## Make it tangible

A filter page. The programmer registers `(rf/reg-route :route/listing {} "/listing")` and builds an address with an 8-, 9- and 12-key query map. What `route-url` emits TODAY versus under (B) (probe 1, JVM, trunk 634b085f12; keys sorted alphabetically under (B) because all are keywords):

```
8 keys   TODAY: /listing?cat=furniture&dir=asc&max=500&min=10&page=2&q=chair&size=50&sort=name
         (B)  : identical

9 keys   TODAY: /listing?cat=furniture&q=chair&min=10&color=oak&dir=asc&page=2&size=50&max=500&sort=name
         (B)  : /listing?cat=furniture&color=oak&dir=asc&max=500&min=10&page=2&q=chair&size=50&sort=name

12 keys  TODAY: /listing?cat=furniture&q=chair&min=10&color=oak&dir=asc&page=2&size=50&brand=acme&ship=au&max=500&sort=name&instock=true
         (B)  : /listing?brand=acme&cat=furniture&color=oak&dir=asc&instock=true&max=500&min=10&page=2&q=chair&ship=au&size=50&sort=name
```

Today's 9- and 12-key strings are stable (same map, any spelling → same string) but visibly unsorted. Nothing the programmer dispatches, subscribes to, or matches behaves differently between the two rows. What differs is what they READ in the address bar and what the spec told them to expect.

Under (A) the sentence they read becomes (proposed wording, one clause changed):

> `match-url(route-url(...))` returns canonical route data, query keys are emitted in a deterministic order that does not depend on how the caller spelled the map (canonical CEDN-1 key order up to eight keys), `nil` query values are elided, …

Under (B) the sentence stays, and the three sites become:

```clojure
;; registry.cljc:1032-1033, :1113-1115, :1849-1852 — each `(into (array-map) xs)` becomes
(apply array-map (mapcat identity xs))
```

## Options

### A. Reword the promise to what the code does (doc-only)
- What changes: `spec/Conventions.md:1054` one clause (wording above, or shorter: "in a deterministic, spelling-independent order"); `docs/api/re-frame.routing.md:111` and `:136` to match; `registry.cljc` docstring :1007-1009 and comments :1021, :1826-1839 kept in step (the docstring's "return an array-map so the order is stable downstream" becomes "stable up to eight keys; a larger map promotes to a hash map whose order is still spelling-independent"). The four fixture/test comments and the property-test header quote the sentence and should follow the new wording in the same PR, so a `deterministic canonical order` census reads 0 outside `.beads` afterwards (control today: 14 lines / 9 files). No code line moves.
- Consequences: programmer — nothing observable changes; the spec stops promising a sorted query string above 8 keys and keeps promising the property they rely on (same map → same URL). AI writing against the API — reads a true sentence instead of a false one. Tools — none read the order. Production — nil. Spec — one clause in a hot-zone file; 012 untouched.
- Cost: under one worker-morning. Files: `spec/Conventions.md` (HOT ZONE, one-toucher), `docs/api/re-frame.routing.md`, `registry.cljc` (docstrings/comments only), two fixture comments, two test comments. Gates: `check_doc_slugs.py` + `python -m mkdocs build --strict` (staged `spec/` and `docs/api`), lint's `api-manifest` job (docs/api is on its path filter; it grades names, so prose passes), routing JVM lane as a docstring-only reader check. Neither link gate reads prose, so the worker says so in the PR body.
- Risk: low. The only trap is wording that re-promises something false in the other direction (cross-host byte identity is unmeasured; do not add it). Dropping "canonical" leaves no trace in the tree, which is why the bead refused to let a sweep land it — the ruling itself is the trace.

### B. Keep the promise and make it true (one line per site)
- What changes: `(into (array-map) …)` → `(apply array-map (mapcat identity …))` at `registry.cljc:1032`, `:1113`, `:1849`. Every comment and spec sentence above becomes TRUE as written, so nothing in prose moves. The lock: raise the property test's `gen-query` bound from `(rnd state 4)` to e.g. `(rnd state 13)` (:118) so its 300 + 200 seeded draws cover 9-12 keys on BOTH hosts (its docstring :38-40 says it draws the same stream on CLJ and CLJS), plus one 9-key example in `routing_registry_test.clj` and, if wanted, one 9-key conformance fixture row.
- Consequences: programmer — emitted URL strings for 9+ query keys change to sorted order (the (B) rows above); anything that stored a pre-change URL string (a bookmark, a cached href, a test expectation) no longer byte-matches the new emission for the same map. Pre-alpha and unreleased, so no external consumer exists yet. `match-url`'s `:query` for 9+ keys becomes a >8-entry `PersistentArrayMap`; an app `assoc` on it promotes to a hash map as ordinary Clojure does. AI/tools — a sorted query string is easier to read and diff. Spec — nothing moves.
- Cost: under one worker-morning. Files: `registry.cljc` (3 lines), `routing_prism_property_cljs_test.cljc` (1 number), `routing_registry_test.clj` (1 example). No hot-zone file. Gates: routing JVM lane (`clojure -M:test`, 66 tests / 408 assertions in that ns per rf2-17bbi's report) and the CLJS lane.
- Risk: two small ones, neither litigation-worthy. (1) The worker's "holds at any size" was verified on the JVM only; CLJS `array-map` is expected to behave the same but is UNMEASURED here — the raised property bound is what settles it in the same PR. (2) The invariant is fragile by construction: a `PersistentArrayMap` past 8 entries re-promotes on the next `assoc`, so a fourth site that ever `assoc`es after the sort silently reintroduces the drift; the three sites are terminal today (iterated, never assoc'ed), and the raised property bound is the only guard.

## Recommendation

**(A).** Argued from the stance:

- Nothing observable is wrong. Matching, validation, defaults, no-op detection and same-map-same-URL all hold at 12 keys on a real route (measured). The only thing that is false is a clause in a spec sentence, and the fix for a false sentence is a true sentence.
- "Trust the programmer": a programmer who wants a sorted query string above 8 keys can see in the address bar that they do not have one, and nothing they build on re-frame2 needs one. A promise that exists to be tidy rather than to be relied upon is exactly the kind of guarantee the stance says not to gold-plate.
- "Don't litigate the minutiae": (B) is cheap, but it is a behaviour change to a public URL surface, carries an unmeasured CLJS half, and installs an invariant that a future `assoc` silently breaks — three things to keep true for a property with no consumer. (A) is one clause and leaves the code, tests and fixtures alone.
- The mayor's counter — a guarantee is cheapest to drop now — is right about timing but overstates what is dropped. The guarantee consumers build on (spelling-independent, stable URL for a given map) is KEPT under (A); only the word "canonical" past 8 keys goes.

What would change my mind: if Mike wants SSR-rendered hrefs with 9+ query keys to match the client's re-render as a STATED cross-host guarantee, take (B) — under (A) that parity rests on JVM and CLJS hash-map iteration agreeing (a Clojure design fact nobody here has measured), whereas under (B) it rests on a sort. Or if he simply wants sorted, hand-readable query strings as a product property: (B) is three lines and the raised property bound, and no hot-zone file.

## Codex Recommendation

**Choose B: keep canonical query ordering and repair the three existing constructions.** For a pre-alpha SPA library, a consistent URL is a useful default that costs the programmer nothing. This is a small implementation correction with no new API, option, dependency, or caller obligation. I would not expose an eight-key exception in the public contract.

**Independent findings.** I researched revision `6a3bf87c1885ef66531bc70eb64378a52f6e41fc`; the relevant source, property test and Conventions file had no working-tree differences from that revision. I read `bd show rf2-c5cub` and its history as background, then checked the implementation and examples independently.

- The promise remains in `spec/Conventions.md:1054` and the public reference at `docs/api/re-frame.routing.md:111,136`. Inbound ordering was deliberately added by commit `0d78ba6e2c81b03ac9cfa5c5453de017bc222b4b`, rather than appearing accidentally in a later comment.
- `implementation/routing/src/re_frame/routing/registry.cljc:1032` and `:1849` sort into an array-map. The third site, `:1113`, does **not** sort: it rebuilds the already ordered map while removing defaults. URL serialization subsequently iterates that result at `:2220–2231`. Each reconstruction therefore matters to the proposed repair.
- My read-only JVM probe used the current routing source with Clojure 1.12.4 and a registered `/listing` route. For both keyword and string keys named `k01` onward, eight entries emitted in canonical order; nine and twelve did not. Reversing construction order produced the same URL, and matching preserved the expected query data. Separately, feeding `query-without-defaults` an explicitly ordered twelve-entry map and removing one default produced an unordered eleven-entry result.
- An independent Node probe loaded only the existing compiled ClojureScript 1.12.145 core runtime. At eight, nine and twelve entries, `(apply array-map ...)` preserved the supplied order for both key types; the `into` construction lost it above eight. The observed hash-map orders also matched the JVM for these samples. This closes the narrow constructor uncertainty; it does not establish universal cross-host URL or hydration behavior. The [versioned ClojureScript implementation](https://github.com/clojure/clojurescript/blob/r1.12.145/src/main/cljs/cljs/core.cljs) corroborates the constructor behavior.

**Practical significance.** I found no reason to elevate this into a navigation failure. No-op detection uses map equality (`implementation/routing/src/re_frame/routing/plan.cljc:94–97`), and the inspected RealWorld route has only `:feed` and `:page` (`examples/real-apps/realworld_http/routing.cljs:48–58`). A richer filter screen is a plausible beneficiary, not an observed broken application. The improvement is predictable, readable URLs and a promise that remains simple as a screen grows. A caller cannot obtain that merely by supplying an ordered map: `route-url` reconstructs it at `:1849`.

**Options and tradeoffs.** A is defensible if query presentation has no product value: removing the promise avoids any runtime change. But it leaves sorting work in place while discarding its result above an incidental collection threshold, and requires weakening several public explanations. B changes the spelling of affected URLs, so exact-string expectations may need updating; their route data remains equivalent in the cases measured. Pre-alpha is a reasonable time to make that small change. Keeping the existing CEDN-1 ordering is enough; there is no need for another ordering policy or configurable serializer.

**Scope and validation.** Use the existing three-site approach, including the defaults rebuild, and add a compact shared-host regression covering explicit eight-, nine- and twelve-distinct-key cases, with a defaults case that still leaves more than eight emitted keys. Check emitted order, inbound key order and unchanged values. The current property generator draws at most three pairs (`implementation/routing/test/re_frame/routing_prism_property_cljs_test.cljc:114–127`); raising its bound is useful supplementary coverage, but fixed boundary examples make the regression clear. The [Clojure data-structure reference](https://clojure.org/reference/data_structures#ArrayMaps) documents that further association can promote an array-map, so the guarantee should concern library output, without promising that later caller transformations retain it.

Both probes exited 0. I ran no routing test suite, browser hydration test, benchmark, or newly compiled CLJS routing build, and made no implementation changes. The CLJS observation is specifically about the existing core artifact and the proposed map construction. That is sufficient evidence for this recommendation; the implementation change should still run its focused routing tests on both hosts.

title: Incomplete: Story-MCP success projection retains callable record extension keys
description:
PR #9759 (f0c34b18c77744d05f5ffe563490df86db05e95f) incompletely satisfies closed rf2-gwye.58's requirement that supported success values are projected without raw #object identities. The ordinary predicate-assertion repair works; this is a separate, narrower record-extension-key omission.

Location: tools/story-mcp/src/re_frame/story_mcp/tools/result.cljc, wire-safe-success (postwalk at lines 154-159), applied by edn-result.

Reproducer using the landed source:
(defrecord Sample [v])
(story/reg-story :story.audit {})
(story/reg-variant* :story.audit/record
  {:args {:record (assoc (->Sample pos?) pos? :extension)}})
After ordinary plain-atom initialization, invoke get-variant for story.audit/record through server/run-loop!, with max-tokens 0. Both dedup true and false return successful encoded frames whose text contains the original #object callable key and its JVM identity. The :v field is correctly projected to the bounded marker, so the omission is specifically the extension key, not a failure to run the projection.

Cause: clojure.walk/postwalk rebuilds a record by conjoining transformed entries into the ORIGINAL record. A changed extension key is added under its marker while the old callable key remains. Direct wire-safe-success confirms contains? on the original pos? key is still true. Cheshire then emits the surviving key/identity, and the text contains non-data despite the new bounded-marker contract. P3: uncommon but valid registered author data produces unstable, unprojected output; this is not a protocol failure or a general security-boundary claim.

Required correction: preserve record identity/ordinary fields while removing original extension keys whose projected key changes before inserting their replacements. Reuse the small record-rebuild approach already present in the shared MCP codec where appropriate; no new general serialization layer or API is needed.

Validation: actual source URL printed, changed source matches the merge, direct collection/literal-key controls pass, and a real registered get-variant through run-loop! confirms #object in the encoded response and text for both dedup settings. Local evidence: C:/Users/miket/.codex/tmp/audit-re-frame2-pr9759-projection-probe-1.{clj,log,exit} and audit-re-frame2-pr9759-record-wire-probe-1.{clj,log,exit}, both exit 0. These are characterization probes, not passing regression tests. Existing CI passes 301 tests / 1709 assertions and does not cover a transformed record extension key.

Deduplication: all 50 literal-open Beads checked (unlimited and explicit high limit); no existing open item explicitly records this defect and correction. The source is closed and remains closed. No mayor notification or acknowledgment is inferred from this filing or its push.
acceptance_criteria: A registered variant containing a record with a callable or opaque extension key crosses get-variant with dedup both on and off without retaining the original key or emitting #object identities. Confirm the replacement marker is present, ordinary record fields/type and data-only collection shapes remain intact, and the existing predicate/exception wire tests pass.
notes:
FIXED in PR #9784 (branch worker/storyrec-a, commit e5bfb87c1c). Filed from the merged-PR audit of #9759 (closed rf2-gwye.58, which stays closed).

Cause, confirmed at source at trunk 9a125db2ca: wire-safe-success in tools/story-mcp/src/re_frame/story_mcp/tools/result.cljc walked with clojure.walk/postwalk. That function rebuilds a RECORD by conj-ing the walked entries back into the ORIGINAL record. So an extension key the projection respells, such as a pos? key, gained its bounded marker while the raw callable key stayed beside it, and Cheshire emitted that key with its identity string.

Where the rebuild came from: wire-safe-success now walks with clojure.walk/walk everywhere except a record, which goes through a local rebuild-record. That helper is a COPY of the private rebuild-record in re-frame.mcp-base.dedup, the rf2-gwye.31 fix for the same hazard in the dedup walk. It is copied rather than called because it is ^:private in another artefact, and that codec is outside this bead's fence. mcp-base is unchanged. The helper rebuilds every entry first, dissocs any key whose spelling changed, then writes the rebuilt entries back, so the record keeps its type and fixed fields. There is no new API and no new serialization layer, and nothing outside tools/story-mcp/** changed.

What the regression pins (tools/story-mcp/test/re_frame/story_mcp/wire_encodability_test.clj):
- record-extension-key-crosses-get-variant-as-a-marker is the bead's reproducer: a defrecord Sample with a pos? extension key, registered through reg-story and reg-variant*. It drives get-variant through the real run-loop! with dedup true and false, and checks four things. First, no #object appears in the encoded frame or its text, and neither does a pos_QMARK_@ identity string or any identity hash. Second, the structured record carries exactly its two entries. Fourth, the data-only list, set and vector are unchanged and keep their collection types.
- wire-safe-success-drops-a-record-key-it-respells is a direct unit guard plus a type-preservation control. The control covers a record with a plain extension key, a sorted map and nested lists.

- The existing predicate and exception wire tests still pass.

The bead's both-settings acceptance is exercised as written, but the mcp-base dedup walk itself is not on this path; that walk already carries its own record fix (rf2-gwye.31).

title: xray: tools/xray/deps.edn declares stock Reagent for a reason PR #9686 removes, and its comment was already stale
description:
FOUND BY `slimfix-a` WHILE REPAIRING rf2-7ds8 (PR #9686), REPORTED RATHER THAN ABSORBED -- the right
call, since it is a bundle concern rather than a correctness one and widening a bounded repair is how
a bounded repair stops being bounded.

## THE DEFECT

`tools/xray/deps.edn` declared stock Reagent as a dependency BECAUSE Xray's sources required
`reagent.core` directly, to cross into the surviving Reagent islands. The consequence: a page built on
reagent-slim that also carries Xray shipped BOTH ratom runtimes.

PR #9686 reduces this to ONE production require -- the fallback arm -- by routing the crossing through
the installed adapter's `:adapter/as-element` instead of a hardcoded stock-Reagent walk. So after that
change lands the correctness half is gone and what remains is whether the declared dependency is still
warranted for the fallback alone, and whether a slim page still pays for a runtime it does not use.

## A SECOND, SMALLER THING IN THE SAME FILE

The worker reports that the comment in `tools/xray/deps.edn` explaining the Reagent dependency names a
reason that was ALREADY STALE before #9686 touched it. A comment giving a superseded reason is worse
than none -- it will stop the next reader doing something that works. Correct it to say what is
actually true after #9686, or remove it.

## SEQUENCING

**Blocked behind PR #9686.** This bead is about the residue that change leaves, so it cannot be
measured until it lands. Re-derive the require count at that tip rather than trusting the numbers
above -- the count in rf2-7ds8's own description was already wrong once (it said five sources; the
measured answer is six sources, nine sites).

## WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS A NON-ITEM

A verified "the fallback arm genuinely needs the dependency and the bundle cost is unavoidable" is a
complete outcome, recorded as the close reason. This is explicitly NOT a mandate to remove the
dependency -- only to establish whether it is still earning its place, and to fix the comment either
way. The project's stance is against gold plating; a bundle-size item with no measured cost attached
is exactly the shape that turns into gold plating, so measure the cost before proposing work.
close_reason:
DONE — PR #9692 merged (docs(xray): say what the stock-Reagent dep actually costs), 87/87 at head
c26d352329, rebased onto main at ba624dfbf4.

The bead's framing was that PR #9686 removes the reason `tools/xray/deps.edn` declares stock Reagent.
Measured rather than argued, and the answer changed the disposition: the dep stays, and what was
missing was a statement of what it COSTS.

What the measurement established:

* The both-runtimes cost is `machines-viz`'s chart tree, NOT the Reagent/Fresco crossings. The
  crossings were the natural suspect and they are not the carrier.
* The bundle cost of the fallback arm is ZERO — it is dead weight only in the sense of a declared
  coordinate, not of shipped bytes.

So the deliverable is the comment in `tools/xray/deps.edn` saying which of those two things the
declaration is paying for, so the next reader does not re-derive it or delete it on the assumption
that the crossings were the cost. The stale comment this bead cited as needing a fix had already
been fixed by #9686 itself; that half of the premise did not hold and is recorded here rather than
re-opened.

title: xray: three managed-fx record sections are permanently collapsed — disclosure glyph with no caller-side wiring
description:
THREE SECTIONS OF THE MANAGED-FX RECORD PANEL ARE PERMANENTLY COLLAPSED. The panel collects the
data, renders a "collapsed" disclosure glyph, and the user has no way to open it -- so REQUEST,
RESPONSE and HANDLER DISPATCHED are never visible.

MAYOR-VERIFIED AT SOURCE, trunk c416178b7a, with a nonsense control reading zero:

  theme/section.cljc:86   `section-row` renders its body under `(when expanded? ...)`
  theme/section.cljc      the `header` fn draws `(if expanded? "\u25bc" "\u25b6")` -- a real glyph
  panels/managed_fx_template.cljs:368  {:label "REQUEST"           :expanded? false}
  panels/managed_fx_template.cljs:373  {:label "WIRE TIMING"       :expanded? true }
  panels/managed_fx_template.cljs:378  {:label "RESPONSE"          :expanded? false}
  panels/managed_fx_template.cljs:383  {:label "HANDLER DISPATCHED":expanded? false}
  panels/managed_fx_template.cljs:388  {:label "APP-DB SLICE TOUCHED" :expanded? true}

Those three are LITERAL `false`, and nothing in the panel can change them.

=== THE COMPONENT IS NOT BROKEN, AND THIS IS THE HALF THAT DECIDES THE FIX ===

`theme/section.cljc:52` states the contract outright:

    "No interactivity. Click-to-toggle wiring is the caller's [responsibility]"

So `section-row` is DELIBERATELY non-interactive and needs no repair. **And a working caller
already exists in this tree**: `panels/cancellation_cascade.cljs:689` passes

    :expanded? (rf.fresco/sub [:rf.xray/cancellation-cascade-expanded?])

i.e. a SUBSCRIPTION, with the open/closed state owned by the caller exactly as the contract says.
`managed_fx_template.cljs` simply never did that half.

**THE FIX IS THEREFORE TO COPY AN IN-TREE PATTERN, NOT TO INVENT ONE** -- give the managed-fx
panel its own expansion state and sub, per section, the way the cascade panel does. Do not add
interactivity to `section-row`; that would break its stated contract and its other caller.

=== A CLAIM TO NOT CARRY FORWARD ===

This was surfaced by the rf2-twil worker (tracefx-a), whose report said "nothing in this tree
wires a click -- section-row has no handler and no expansion state anywhere". **The second half is
wrong**: `cancellation_cascade.cljs:689` is expansion state, wired through a sub. The CONCLUSION
held -- those three sections never open, and the four HD-016 vectors inside them never reach a
rendered tree -- but the stated reason would send a repairer off to build wiring from scratch with
a working example one file away. Recorded because the conclusion was right and the reason was not,
which is the harder case to catch.

=== CONSEQUENCE FOR THE HD-016 HAZARD, WHICH IS WHY THIS WAS FOUND ===

`body` is a positional argument, so the collapsed body IS constructed and then discarded by the
`when`. Constructing a hiccup VECTOR calls nothing, so the four `[edn/inspect ...]` head-position
sites in this file cannot throw at runtime while their sections stay shut -- which is why no test
tier ever graded them, and why an HD-016 regression row over that subtree reads zero rather than
going red on a revert. **Wiring the disclosure makes those four sites reachable**, so whoever takes
this bead must land it AFTER, or together with, the head-form repair in rf2-twil / rf2-fcy5 --
otherwise opening the sections is what turns a latent hazard into a live throw.
notes:
=== CARRIED ACROSS FROM rf2-s6m6, closed as a duplicate of this bead (rf2-twil worktree) ===

SCOPE. `theme/section/section-row` is SHARED with `panels/event_detail` (per its own ns
docstring). Because the primitive is deliberately dumb -- "Click-to-toggle wiring is the
caller's responsibility" -- the expansion state belongs in the CALLER, which is exactly what
`panels/cancellation_cascade.cljs:689` already demonstrates. So this is a per-panel change and
NOT a change to the shared widget. Do not add expansion state to `section.cljc` by reflex; two
panels would then inherit it.

WHICH READ TO USE DEPENDS ON WHEN THIS LANDS. cancellation_cascade's working example wires
`:expanded?` with `rf.fresco/sub` from inside a `defview` -- the migrated world. Today
managed_fx_template's mount (`panels/ManagedFxList`, panels.cljs:430) is still an `rf/reg-view`,
so a pre-migration repair reads with `@(rf/subscribe …)` and a post-migration one with
`rf.fresco/sub`. Check which side you are on before copying the example.

WASTED WORK, NOT ONLY A DEAD AFFORDANCE. The three collapsed bodies are positional arguments
to `section-row`, so they are evaluated on every render and then discarded -- including the
edn-inspector vectors, the costliest thing on the panel.

SEQUENCING, and it is the reason this bead matters beyond UX: wiring the disclosure is what
turns managed_fx_template's four `edn/inspect` sites into gradeable render paths. Nothing can
grade a discarded body, which is the complete explanation for why three tiers of coverage
missed the HD-016 hazard there. So this must land AFTER or WITH rf2-twil's head-form repair
(PR #9624) -- landing it first would make four HD-016 vectors reachable.
close_reason:
DUPLICATE of rf2-s6m6, which the rf2-twil worker filed from the same measurement minutes before I
filed this one. I did not see it because I was verifying the finding at source while it was being
written.

rf2-s6m6 is kept because its evidence is stronger: it quotes the managed-fx panel's OWN docstring
-- "REQUEST + RESPONSE + HANDLER DISPATCHED collapsed by default (one click reveals the payload --
keeps the panel scannable on first paint)" -- which is the code documenting the very behaviour that
is missing. That is better than anything this bead had.

Everything this bead carried that rf2-s6m6 did not has been APPENDED to it rather than lost:
  - `theme/section.cljc:52`, the stated contract that the non-interactivity is DELIBERATE and
    click-to-toggle wiring belongs to the caller
  - `panels/cancellation_cascade.cljs:689`, a caller in this tree that already does it through
    `(rf.fresco/sub [:rf.xray/cancellation-cascade-expanded?])`
  - the consequent narrowing of "nothing anywhere wires a toggle", which is true per-file and
    false about the tree, and which would otherwise send a repairer to build from scratch
  - the sequencing constraint against PR #9624

Closed as a duplicate rather than worked, so two workers cannot be dispatched at one finding --
the second time this pair of instruments has produced a duplicate today (rf2-2rn3 / rf2-jzv2 was
the first), which is worth noticing as a pattern rather than twice as a coincidence: a worker's
report and the mayor's verification of that report can both end in a bead.

title: False setup-isolation claim: source walks still run after failed prerequisites
description:
Merged-PR audit of #9610 (8814f3c5e52dd8e932ce9e5bb27e75c2d96a1309), correctness lens. The independent-walk repair works: the real deliberate-failure GitHub job 102774846596 shows the first walk failing and all six later walks succeeding. This follow-up concerns the distinct setup-failure boundary claimed by rf2-gf3y and the new test.yml:3203-3206 comment.

All seven walk conditions are solely ${{ !cancelled() }} (test.yml:3208 onward). None checks that checkout/JDK/Clojure installation succeeded. Leaving setup steps themselves at their implicit success() condition does not restore that prerequisite on later steps. GitHub explicitly says a status-check function replaces the implicit success() check; cancelled() reports cancellation, not preceding failure: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/expressions#status-check-functions . Consequently a failed checkout or CLI installation still selects every walk, producing seven missing-directory/tool failures rather than the one setup failure the comment promises. This is a source-and-documented-semantics counterexample, not a claim to have injected a setup failure into CI. The job remains red; this does not admit a bad merge.

The paired _changed-surfaces.test.cjs assertion currently permits only the exact !cancelled() spelling, so it also rejects a prerequisite-success conjunct. Repair that narrow boundary together with its pin: require successful essential setup while retaining cancellation handling and independence from previous WALK failures. A single setup-ready marker or equivalent explicit step outcome check suffices; no new CI framework. Fresh census of 25 literal-open Beads found no exact owner for this defect. Original rf2-gf3y remains closed; its status, criteria and normative close reason are preserved.
acceptance_criteria: Demonstrate both branches: after successful prerequisites and an intentionally failed first walk, the six later walks execute and the job remains failed; after a failed essential setup step, the seven walks are skipped. Cancellation still skips walks, no path-based/job-level gate is introduced, and each namespace retains its separate invocation/floor. Update the paired structural pin and comments to match these conditions without adding a general workflow abstraction.
notes:
PR #9618 opened and GREEN (87 checks: 83 success, 4 skipped, 0 failed, 0 pending;
4 workflow runs at head f6295fe18d6a1b74dce3a8d6d0fc70a8a97dab4e all
completed/success). Branch worker/setupgate-b. Adds no job key.

REPAIR. A new `Essential setup complete` marker step (`id: setup`) sits between
the Clojure CLI install and the Maven cache, carrying nothing but GitHub's
default `success()`, so its outcome reaches `success` only when the checkout,
the JDK install and the Clojure CLI install all did — a step skipped by a
failure ahead of it reports `skipped`, not `success`, so one id covers all
three. The seven walks now read
`if: ${{ !cancelled() && steps.setup.outcome == 'success' }}`, which satisfies
both requirements at once: a failed prerequisite skips them, and a failing walk
still cannot skip the six behind it.

Three sub-calls, each recorded in the workflow comment:
- `outcome` not `conclusion`, so a `continue-on-error:` could not launder a
  failure into a success.
- The marker sits ABOVE the Maven cache: a cache miss is not a reason to skip
  the walks, only to run them slower.
- A separate step rather than an `id:` on the installer step, whose exact
  two-line shape is pinned across ~50 call sites by rf2-e7ja9. That pin fired
  on the first attempt (which did put `id: setup` on the installer step), which
  is how the separate marker was chosen.

The overstated comment is rewritten to say what the conditions actually
guarantee, and cites the status-check-functions URL.

TEST HALF, same commit. `_changed-surfaces.test.cjs` permitted only the bare
`!cancelled()` spelling. It now pins the new spelling, the marker step's
existence, and its position ABOVE the walks. Those last two matter because they
fail OPEN: with the marker deleted or moved below the walks,
`steps.setup.outcome` evaluates to null, `null == 'success'` is false, and all
seven walks SKIP while the job reports GREEN.

VERIFICATION. `node --test implementation/scripts/_changed-surfaces.test.cjs`
read 369 passed. Controlled both ways with three deliberate regressions applied
to the workflow and reverted, each red with its intended message: conditions
trimmed to bare `!cancelled()`, marker step deleted, marker moved below the

title: CLAUDE.md: which git hash-object form matches a committed blob is per-file (i/lf vs i/crlf), and the wrong one reads as a failed restore
description:
WHICH `git hash-object` FORM MATCHES A COMMITTED BLOB IS A PER-FILE FACT, AND THE MAYOR HAS
BEEN BRIEFING IT AS A UNIVERSAL. The wrong form returns a hash that resolves to NO OBJECT IN
THE REPO, which reads as a FAILED RESTORE on a file that was restored perfectly.

DELIVERABLE: a new lettered item in CLAUDE.md's `## Workflow` instrument list. Nothing else.

=== MEASURED BY THE MAYOR AT TIP 03d4af871c, FOUR FILES, BOTH FORMS (fact) ===

    file                                  ls-files --eol   default   --no-filters
    CLAUDE.md                             i/lf  w/crlf     MATCH     no
    spec/011-SSR.md                       i/crlf w/crlf    no        MATCH
    docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md        i/lf  w/crlf     MATCH     no
    scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh           i/lf  w/lf       MATCH     MATCH

"MATCH" means the hash equals `git rev-parse HEAD:<path>`.

**THE DETERMINANT IS THE INDEX SIDE (`i/`), NOT THE WORKING-TREE SIDE.** `i/lf` wants the
DEFAULT form, because the clean filter reproduces the LF blob from a CRLF working file.
`i/crlf` wants `--no-filters`, because the blob itself carries CRLF and the clean filter
would strip it. `i/lf w/lf` accepts either.

**AND THE WORKING-TREE SIDE DOES NOT DISCRIMINATE, WHICH IS THE WHOLE TRAP.** Both
`CLAUDE.md` and `spec/011-SSR.md` read `w/crlf`. That is the half a reader looks at — it is
what you see in an editor and what `core.autocrlf=true` explains — and it is IDENTICAL across
the two files that want OPPOSITE forms. A rule derived from one file and stated as a fact
about "this tree's files" is therefore wrong for half of them, with nothing on screen to say
so.

=== HOW IT FAILS, AND WHY IT IS WORSE THAN A WRONG NUMBER ===

The wrong form returns a well-formed 40-character hash that simply names nothing:
`git cat-file -t <hash>` answers `fatal: could not get object info`. In the act this is used
for — verifying a sabotage restore by blob hash — that reads as **THE RESTORE FAILED**. The
worker then goes looking for damage that does not exist, and `loops.md` already names the cost
in the sentence that prescribes the check: *"a false 'restore failed' sends the worker off to
doubt the sabotage result, which was the deliverable."*

So it fails by DISCREDITING GOOD EVIDENCE rather than by passing bad evidence. That is why it
earns an entry despite being loud: the loudness lands on the wrong conclusion.

=== PROVENANCE, AND STATE IT PLAINLY IN THE ENTRY ===

`loops.md` prescribes "version control's own content hash against the committed object" without
naming a flag — correctly, since it is repository-neutral. The MAYOR then concretised it as
"use `--no-filters`", on a single measurement from `spec/011-SSR.md` relayed by one worker, and
put that spelling into roughly five dispatch briefs this session. The `ghcase-a` worker measured
the opposite on `CLAUDE.md` and said so; the table above is the mayor re-measuring both.

**Write the entry as a concretion of loops.md, not as a discovery, and cite it** — the same
division of labour items (b), (p) and (q) already have. Do not edit `docs/the-mayor-method/**`;
its statement is right as written.

=== THE GUARD — GIVE BOTH FORMS, AND THE ONE-LINE TEST ===

  * Ask the file: `git ls-files --eol <path>`, read the `i/` half, and pick the form.
  * Or skip the question entirely and compare against the object directly:

        git rev-parse "HEAD:<path>"        # the committed blob id
        git hash-object <path>             # default
        git hash-object --no-filters <path>

    and treat a match by EITHER form as a good restore. That is the form to lead with,
    because it needs no rule to be remembered and no attribute to be read.
  * **Never conclude "restore failed" from one form.** Check the other before believing it,
    and `git diff --quiet HEAD -- <path>` is a second independent instrument that answers the
    same question without hashing anything.

=== SCOPE, AND TWO TRAPS SPECIFIC TO THIS FILE ===

CLAUDE.md ONLY. No script, no gate.

  1. **The lettered list's opening sentence warns that a COUNT in it goes stale first, and it
     has been wrong before** — it carried the word FIVE while there were six. Add a letter; do
     NOT add or update any count, and check the surrounding prose carries none you would
     invalidate.
  2. **Item (e) records a CRLF trap about editing this exact file**, and item (o) records that
     the Bash tool HALVES backslash runs inside a quoted heredoc. Your entry quotes shell
     commands. After editing: total CR count must equal the CRLF count, `git check-attr text --
     CLAUDE.md` must still read `text: unspecified` with `i/lf w/crlf`, and `git diff --stat`
     must show the lines you actually changed rather than 156. **Report all three numbers in
     the PR body.**

=== GATES ===

`scripts/check_readme_links.py --ci` owns repo-root markdown, CLAUDE.md included.
`scripts/check_doc_slugs.py` does NOT — its roots are `docs/`, `spec/`, `skills/`, `migration/`
and `tools/*/spec`, and it exits 0 on a broken link outside them. Both run in `test.yml`'s
`verify-readme-links` job, whose NAME reads as though it checks READMEs while the gate that
actually does is the other one. Nominate by PATH. `mkdocs build --strict` does NOT cover
CLAUDE.md at all — `docs_dir` is `docs`. Do not nominate it.

Plus `check_retired_composition_vocab.py` (it rosters CLAUDE.md explicitly),
`check_retired_spellings.py`, and the attribution guard, which grades BOTH your commits and the
PR BODY and reads that body from the FROZEN EVENT PAYLOAD — a re-run re-reads the old text for
ever, so get it right the first time.

SABOTAGE: plant a broken link target on a line you added, show `check_readme_links.py --ci`
going red naming file and target, restore, and verify by blob hash — **using the form this bead
is about, and say which one and why.** That is the entry proving itself.
